Written and maintained by CASRAI Editorial Board

This guide provides an informational overview of clinical software, imaging workflows, and regulatory standards. It does not provide medical advice or individual patient diagnostic instructions.

Radiology artificial intelligence refers to computer vision and machine learning algorithms trained to acquire, optimize, analyze, and triage diagnostic medical images. Rather than replacing medical specialists, these software tools function as clinical decision support. They detect anomalies, measure anatomical structures, prioritize emergent cases, and export structured findings into imaging networks under human physician supervision.

Radiology artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses software algorithms—predominantly deep neural networks—trained to process diagnostic images across modalities including X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound. Its clinical scope spans the imaging life cycle from scan acquisition through post-scan interpretation.

In clinical workflows, image files conform to the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine standard. When an imaging study completes, AI software reads the series, extracts features, and generates quantitative outputs such as bounding boxes around suspicious findings, lesion segmentations, or prioritized worklist flags. Under consensus statements from professional imaging societies, clinical AI operates as an assistive technology: licensed radiologists retain sole diagnostic responsibility for interpreting findings and signing the final report.

Several frequent misconceptions surround the implementation of artificial intelligence in radiology:

Computer-Aided Detection (CADe) marks suspicious regions to prevent perceptual oversight. Computer-Assisted Diagnosis (CADx) provides characterization metrics (such as probability of malignancy) for an already detected lesion. Computer-Assisted Triage and Notification (CADt) analyzes images in the background to identify acute emergencies and prioritize them in the review queue.

Under the Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) framework and Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs), manufacturers specify anticipated model modifications during premarket review. This mechanism allows controlled algorithmic updates without requiring an entirely new 510(k) submission for every iterative enhancement.

The licensed interpreting physician retains legal and professional responsibility for the final diagnostic report. Clinical guidelines emphasize that AI tools serve solely as adjunctive decision support; radiologists must independently confirm or reject algorithmic prompts.

Local validation ensures an algorithm performs reliably on a hospital’s specific imaging equipment, slice thickness parameters, and patient demographic mix. Algorithms trained on external datasets can experience performance drops when exposed to novel clinical settings.
